Audiobook metadata matching, compared

7 tools, the same 4,044 audiobooks, every result checked by hand

Each tool was given the same real audiobooks with their original, never-edited tags and asked to find each book's listing and write its details. Then every result was checked: was it the right book, and did the book end up with the right title, author, narrator and series? The checking was done with Claude, an AI model, under human supervision (how).

  • 2026-11-04
  • 4,044 books
  • 7 tools
  • LibraForge build 527247d

The tools

How each one matches and writes, which also decides what "correct" means for it, with our notes from running it.

LibraForge

public catalog + Goodreads
Matches against
Audible public catalog (no login), with Goodreads when Audible has no good listing
How
Reads the tags, the folder path and the runtime together, runs several searches (the file's ASIN, title and author, keywords) and scores every candidate on title, author, narrator, series, book number and runtime.
Review
Applies confident matches and holds the rest for review, with the reason
Writes
Writes the listing's fields to the files. When the runtime or the narrator says the file is another recording, keeps the file's narrator, ASIN, year and ISBN. A series-only match writes the series alone.
Speed
11 min for 4,044 books, 5 at once (yes, Search workers 1 to 30)

Works best with the Goodreads fallback on, which finds books Audible lists badly or not at all. When the runtime or narrator says a file is another recording of the book, it keeps the file's own narrator instead of writing the listing's. 0 of the 34 books it held for review were the wrong pick.

AudioSilo

Matches against
Its own community database (audiosilo-meta, CC0), not Audible
How
Sends the path, the tags and the runtime together. Books whose tags carry an ASIN or ISBN are matched at scan. Applies a match only at score 90 or more, 10 ahead of the next candidate, with an ASIN or ISBN and the runtime within 10%.
Review
Holds everything else for review
Writes
A confident match attaches the ASIN and fills only blank fields, so the file's title, narrator and series stay. Everything else waits in review.
Speed
1 min for 4,044 books with its local copy of the database, 13 min against its online service; 2 at once (no, a match run uses 2 workers)

Part of its own metadata project. The whole database can be downloaded locally (mirror mode, about 2 GB, refreshed daily), so matching is fast and never polls their service. Coverage is only what the community has added, and it fills only blank fields, so a file's wrong title or series stays. 526 of the 966 books it held for review were the wrong pick.

Audiobookshelf Quick Match

Matches against
Audible (Audiobookshelf's provider, US store)
How
Quick Match per book: the file's ASIN when it has one, else one search and its first result. No runtime check.
Review
None, applies the first result
Writes
Replaces the book's details with the listing's, in Audiobookshelf's database.
Speed
4 h 44 min for 4,044 books, 1 at once (no, Match All goes one book at a time)

A match is only as good as Audible's first result, so later books of a series often get another book's listing.

BookOrbit

Matches against
Its default providers
How
Library bulk metadata fetch.
Review
None
Writes
Fetches the listing into its own records (title, authors, narrators, series), not into the files.
Speed
15 h 53 min for 4,044 books, 1 at once (no, 2 to 5 s pause between books)

Slow by design: 2 to 5 seconds between books. Titles often differ from the book's own.

Grimmory

Matches against
Audible (switched on and put first), then Goodreads, then Google
How
Per provider, one keyword search and its first result; the file's ASIN when its tags carry one (it reads the iTunes copies of the tags, which carry none here).
Review
None
Writes
Fills or replaces each field from the provider's top result, field by field.
Speed
4 h 23 min for 4,044 books, 1 at once (no, one book at a time, providers in turn)

Audible is off by default. No runtime check, so later books in a series often get Book 1.

ReadMeABook

Matches against
Audible
How
Bulk Import scan: one search on the album, album artist and composer tags, first result.
Review
None
Writes
Picks a listing per book and writes nothing, to files or a library. Scored on whether the pick is the book.
Speed
1 h 41 min for 4,044 books, 1 at once (no, 1.5 s pause between searches)

Groups folders by their tags, so a series sharing one album tag is folded into a single book. Reads no series.

beets

audible plugin
Matches against
Audible (beets-audible plugin)
How
beet import -q with the plugin's recommended settings, scoring candidates on track length.
Review
Quiet mode skips anything that isn't a strong match
Writes
Writes the listing's fields to the files when it accepts the match; skips the rest.
Speed
50 min for 4,044 books, 1 per import (4 run) at once (only by running several imports)

Cautious: most of what it writes is the right book, but it writes under half the library. It can't read a file's ASIN from the iTunes tags.

Why AudioSilo matched every book in about a minute

The other tools ask a web service for every book: each search is a round trip to Audible or Goodreads, often several per book, and most pause between books so they aren't blocked. AudioSilo's mirror mode downloads its whole community database once (about 320,000 recordings in one file), so matching is a query on the same disk, with no network and nothing to wait for. The trade-off is coverage: it can only find what the community has added.

Run against its online service instead, the same 4,044 books took 13 min: every book's lookup then makes the round trip to the service.

Where LibraForge went wrong

Of the 3,942 books LibraForge wrote, 3,831 came out fully correct and 0 were the wrong book. The rest were the right book with something off:

  • 21No narrator written: the file had none and the match didn't supply one (mostly Goodreads, which lists no narrators)
  • 18A box set's range cut off the title ("Box Set (25-28)" written as "Box Set")
  • 18A series written without its book number, though the file or folder had it
  • 16Another recording's narrator written on a file that had no narrator tag
  • 16One book number written on a multi-book set
  • 6No series written for a book in one
  • 4A co-author missing
  • 4The series name written as the title
  • 3The series left on the end of the title ("9d6 (Caverns & Creatures)")
  • 3The wrong book number
  • 3Another title written (a Goodreads edition, or one story of a collection)
  • 2The author's name in the narrator field taken for another recording, and kept as the narrator
  • 2A decimal book number (3.5, 14.5) dropped

How it was tested

4,044 audiobooks in their original state, before any matching: the tags LibraForge saved before it first wrote anything to a library's books, or another library's files as they were. Each book was matched again from those original tags, its folder path and its runtime, with no login, against the live catalog.

Every tool got the same books, as silent files carrying the original tags at the books' real folder paths (and, for tools that check runtime, as long as the real book), and each was run the way its own documentation suggests.

How results were judged

Checked with Claude, under human supervision. The book-by-book review was done with Claude, an AI model, following one written set of rules for every tool and every book. A person supervised the work and checked random books by hand along the way, but did not personally review every one of the 4,044 books. The second audit below measures how often the review got a verdict wrong.

Every book and every tool's result on it was audited. Whether a tool picked the right book, another recording of it or the wrong book (and, when it held its pick, whether the held pick was right) was decided by hand, book by book. What the tool then left on the book was checked by script against that tool's own way of writing, so one rule applies to every tool: a field is off when the book ends up with something wrong in it (written, or kept from the file) or without something it is known to have. A tool that keeps the file's own details is judged on the book as it ends up.

To check the audit, 300 random books were audited a second time: 1.8% of verdicts were wrong, and every kind of error found was corrected for all books. A fresh 100 books audited after that had 0.4% wrong, also corrected.

Books Audible's search couldn't show

Audible's search only returns a book where Audible sells it, while looking a book up by its ASIN works everywhere. Some listings are sold in only some of Audible's markets (only the UK and Commonwealth stores, only Australia and New Zealand, only the US and Canada), so a search made outside those markets doesn't return them. Checked against Audible's own sales-rights data, 100 of the 2,979 books with a confirmed listing were hidden from search where these runs were made (2.5% of all books). 79 of those files carry their own ASIN, which a tool can look up directly.

That is the margin of error this adds: run where those books are sold, a tool that searches Audible could do better on at most these 100 books, 2.5% of the library. On them, LibraForge got 98 right, AudioSilo 81 (it reads its own database, so search didn't hide anything from it), Audiobookshelf 87, BookOrbit 88, Grimmory 42, ReadMeABook 37 and beets 17.

Setup per tool
  • LibraForge: Metadata Forge's matcher over the files, Audible public catalog with the Goodreads fallback on, 5 search workers.
  • AudioSilo (v2.5.1): "Match automatically" over the library, in mirror mode (a local copy of the community database). Confident matches count as written, "to review" as held.
  • Audiobookshelf Quick Match (v2.35.1, Audible US provider): Quick Match per book, which takes the first Audible result, or the file's ASIN when it has one. One book at a time, as Match All does.
  • BookOrbit: a library bulk metadata fetch with its default providers.
  • beets (beets 2.14 with the beets-audible plugin, recommended settings): beet import -q, which applies strong matches and skips the rest. It was given each book's real runtime, since it scores on track length.
  • Grimmory (v3.5.0): a library metadata refresh with Audible enabled and first for every field (Goodreads, then Google behind it), applied without review.
  • ReadMeABook (v1.2.12): the Bulk Import scan, which picks an Audible match per book. It groups folders by their tags, so books it merged into another folder count as nothing written. Its scan returns no series.
